name: Black Pudding Toad in the Hole with Apple & Mustard Gravy
why: Peak autumn British cooking — black pudding is at its best right now, and turning it into a giant tear-and-share toad in the hole with a warming apple-and-mustard gravy is a proper crowd-pleasing twist on the classic. Most of the work is the oven's; the batter just needs to rest overnight.
source: Family Home Cook (base recipe), gravy by Henry
author: Henry
ingredients: 2 black pudding wheels (about 200g), cut into nuggets
Vegetable oil, enough to generously coat a roasting tin
2 cooking apples (e.g. Bramley), peeled and roughly chopped

steps: Whisk the milk and eggs together with the salt, then gradually sift in the flour, whisking as you go until smooth. If any lumps remain, pass the batter through a sieve.
Cover and rest the batter in the fridge — minimum 2 hours, but overnight is best. This relaxes the gluten and gives a better rise.
About an hour before cooking, take the batter out of the fridge so it's no longer cold.
Peel and roughly chop the apples, and chop the onion.

Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan). Place a non-stick roasting tin on top of a larger baking tray (to catch overflow) and coat the base with a generous amount of vegetable oil — it should look like too much. That's the point.
Put the tin in the oven for about 10 minutes until the oil is just starting to smoke.
Carefully add the sausages and black pudding nuggets to the smoking oil and roast for 10 minutes until browned on the outside.
Quickly pour the batter in and around the sausages, scatter over the rosemary, and bake for 20–25 minutes until puffed up and a deep golden brown.
While the toad is baking, fry the onion and apples in a little oil (or the fat drained from the tin) over medium heat for about 10 minutes until soft and caramelised at the edges.
Stir in the wholegrain mustard, then pour in the beef stock and a splash of cider if using. Simmer for 5 minutes until slightly thickened.
Taste and season well — it should be sweet, sharp and savoury.
Serve immediately, straight from the tin, spooned with the apple and mustard gravy — ketchup on the side for the purists.

pro_tips: The oil MUST be smoking when the batter hits it — that's the entire secret to the tall, crisp, well-risen pudding. Too much oil, too early, not too little.

Go for proper coarse black pudding (Scottish or Irish style with barley) rather than smooth supermarket rings — the texture is half the appeal. Any leftover batter makes a batch of Yorkshire puddings.
